articles.title: Hilary Swank is having a baby at 52. Why must she defend it?
articles.summary: Hilary Swank's pregnancy at 52 has sparked criticism and invasive questions. Experts and a woman who became a mom at 50 weigh in on the judgment older mother...
articles.body:
Ah, the "joy of pregnancy": Trying to conceive. Worrying about carrying the baby to term. Dealing with morning sickness, awaiting genetic testing results, watching for complications like gestational diabetes and preeclampsia, then — ya know — giving birth.

And if you're an older mother, you may also find yourself defending your decision to have a baby at all against suggestions that you're "selfish" because you may have fewer years with your child. You might also be fielding questions about how you conceived.

Hilary Swank, who's pregnant with her third child at 52, is pushing back on that scrutiny.

"There's a lot of backlash women get for having children older but not men, which is interesting," the Academy Award-winning actor said in a clip of The Drew Barrymore Show that aired Tuesday.

Barrymore replied, "It is weird — men have babies in their 80s, and that is not a euphemism or a joke. You had kids in your 40s [Swank gave birth to twins at age 48] and people weren't always gracious about it."

The women didn't name names in the clip, but actors Robert De Niro and Al Pacino welcomed babies at 79 and 83, respectively, in recent years.

That double standard reflects outdated assumptions about who does the parenting, says Elizabeth Gregory, director of the Institute for Research on Women, Gender & Sexuality at the University of Houston and author of The Real Domestic Product: How Birth Control Built Equality (and Why the Future of the Economy and the Planet Depends on It) .

"Dads are still viewed by many as less essential to their kids, based on old ideas of the gendering of child care that assumed that dads would be less involved," Gregory tells Yahoo.

Swank's announcement comes amid a wave of celebrity baby news from women in their 40s and 50s, including Anne Hathaway , Natalie Portman , Jennifer Meyer and Cameron Diaz . Their circumstances differ, but their experiences raise a broader question: Why are women expected to explain — and sometimes defend — how and when they become mothers?

Swank announced her baby news on Instagram with a joyful video of herself, her husband and their 3-year-old twins doing a literal happy dance. But amid the congratulations, commenters called the Million Dollar Baby star "selfish" because of how old she'll be as her children grow up.

"Imagine being 20 years old and your mother is 72. Honestly this is just selfish," one person wrote.

"52 years old ... bringing a child into your life at such an advanced age??? Just absurd," wrote another.

On the talk show on Tuesday, Swank recalled a story about a woman criticizing an older mother, citing the devastation of losing her father in her early 20s. Swank understood the grief. She was close to her father and took a three-year acting hiatus to be his end-of-life caretaker . But she drew a different conclusion.

"[My dad] was one of my favorite people on earth," Swank said. "I thought to myself, 'Well, I would rather be born and have that person [who] was my favorite person and experience that than not at all.'"

Other commenters felt entitled to private medical information, pressing Swank to disclose fertility treatments.

"I believe you have a responsibility to share the story behind your pregnancy as well," one wrote, arguing that announcements without those details could give other women unrealistic expectations about their fertility.

Swank has previously shared part of that history. She told Women's Health last year that she froze her eggs at 37 and later used them to have her twins, Aya and Ohm, at 48.

That speculation extends beyond fertility treatments. Earlier this year, social media users accused Hathaway of wearing a fake baby bump while pregnant with her third child at 43, prompting a response from the star.

Amid the focus on age and conception, what women say about their actual experience of motherhood can get lost. In her Women's Health interview, Swank described what becoming a parent later allowed her to bring to motherhood.

"I'm a very different parent than I would've been, even in my early 40s," she said. "I'm much more patient. I'm much more understanding. … And I have my career that's already established, so I'm not divided. I'm able to really sink in and be present with them and be a hands-on parent."

Diaz, who welcomed her third child at 53 earlier this year, says motherhood has completely reshaped her view of aging.

"I've got 50 or 60 years to go," she said on the Goop podcast in 2022. "I want to live to be 110, since I've got a young child."

'That kind of pessimism is just horrible'

For professional photographer Danielle Levitt, who became a mother at 50, the suggestion that older mothers are "selfish" hits hard.

"I honestly feel choked up just reading that question, and the first thought that comes up for me is: f*** off," she tells Yahoo. "Pardon my French, but really. That kind of pessimism is just horrible."

Levitt, who shared her experience in a 2025 essay for Glamour , says she didn't deliberately put off motherhood until 50.

"I knew I wasn't ready before then, and I knew I wanted to be in the best place possible to give [my daughter] the best life possible," she says.

While nobody has challenged her to defend her decision, she has encountered "perplexed remarks from people who seem surprised that I am her mom: 'Oh, you're her mother?'" Those comments, she says, touch on socially constructed internalized ageism that "evokes a sense of self-consciousness or embarrassment."

Questions about her experience with in vitro fertilization (IVF), however, are welcome.

"Honestly, I believe in sharing everything so nothing feels intrusive," she says.

At least 10 women have contacted her to say her story inspired them to pursue IVF at an older age, she says. For Levitt, that openness is a way to help others explore their options.

"For those who want to have kids, it's the greatest gift, and if you can have kids and it's something you want, I want people to be empowered to have the same opportunities that I did," she says.

Choosing to share those details is different from being expected to explain them.

Erin Erenberg, CEO of the advocacy organization Chamber of Mothers , sees questions about conception as an extension of the unsolicited commentary pregnant women already receive about their bodies and choices.

"A mother's medical history is between her and her provider," she tells Yahoo. "I wish people were far more curious about how we can better support motherhood than about how a mother conceived."

The scrutiny also overlooks the circumstances that influence when women have children. Relationships, financial stability, careers and access to child care can all factor into that timing.

"There is no universally 'right' time to have a baby," Erenberg says. "Some mothers we talk to are having children later because they want to, but others are having children later because they need to."

Gregory also points to changes in reproductive medicine and longevity: "Women can now have kids later due to IVF and surrogacy; people live longer than they used to (on average) so they're more likely to be around."

While the overall U.S. fertility rate reached a record low in 2024, the birth rate among women ages 40 to 44 rose to its highest level since 1965, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention .

"People bemoan the drop in the fertility rate — but it's largely among young people who are waiting until they feel ready for kids. Many of them will be having their kids later — and as they do, people will get more used to older moms and to caregiving dads of all ages," says Gregory.

Erenberg says that paid leave, affordable child care and maternal health care deserve more attention than a mother's age.

"The energy spent judging older mothers would be far better spent fixing the conditions that make every age the wrong age," she says.

For Levitt, the desire for more time with her daughter exists alongside the certainty that she became a mother when she was ready.

"Do I wish I had all the time in the world with her? Of course, that's all every parent wants," she says. "No wish is greater than having more years with her, but in the end, this was the right time for me to have a child, and I'm really glad I was able to."

articles.title: 21 IIT-Bombay faculty members condemn ‘unprecedented’ police action against protesting students, seek explanation from institute director
articles.summary: 21 IIT-Bombay faculty condemn police detentions of protesting students after Sahil Wakode’s suicide, seeking director’s explanation on authorization and force.
articles.body: MUMBAI: As many as 21 IIT-Bombay faculty members have written to the institute’s director, condemning what they called ‘unprecedented’ police action against students peacefully protesting on campus on Sunday and seeking an explanation.A small section of students have been protesting for over a month after second-year B Tech student Sahil Wakode died by suicide on Sept 18. They have been demanding action and accountability from the institute since then.The letter, sent on Monday, came a day after students were twice detained from the campus protest site, dubbed as ‘Justice Corner’. Police also allegedly dismantled the protest site, removing banners and posters. Sahil’s parents, Ravindra and Sonali Wakode, who visited the institute to pay homage to him alleged they were forcibly taken to Azad Maidan police station and detained till 6pm.The faculty members, in the letter, sought to know whether any institute functionary had authorised police action. If not, they asked whether the administration would seek an FIR against the police officers responsible for the “act of violence” committed against the students.At the outset, the faculty members acknowledged differing views on the ongoing protest, with some considering it irrelevant or damaging to IIT-B’s reputation, while others viewed it as a necessary call for the institute to reflect on its educational commitments and responsibilities amid its history of student suicides. They condemned the forceful removal of students who have been peacefully protesting for several weeks.The faculty members sought explanations from the administration regarding who authorised police to enter the campus and detain students, the use of ‘brute force’ during both rounds of detention, and the alleged failure of institute officials to intervene or help the detainees. “We have learnt that students detained at the police station tried to contact the dean of student affairs, Quick Response Team and chief security officer for help, but their requests were not entertained and that no institute functionary came to the police station. What accounts for it?” they asked.They also questioned the alleged vandalism at the protest site, which displayed images of Jyotirao Phule, Savitribai Phule, and Dr B R Ambedkar. They sought an explanation for the administration’s refusal to return students’ personal belongings, including laptops, and asked whether due procedure had been followed in seizing them.IIT-B authorities did not comment on the letter.Sources claimed that police had come to the campus only because Congress MP Varsha Gaikwad planned to visit that day. The institute had not responded to the MP’s letter seeking permission, and her visit coincided with a visit by Wakode’s parents.Sources also claimed that students jeering at police minutes before Gaikwad and Wakode’s parents arrived had prompted the detentions. Regarding the confiscation of personal belongings, they claimed that the items were lying at the gate and blocking the entrance. articles.title: US orders departure of personnel from Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi threat
articles.summary: US State Department says Iran-aligned Houthis have ‘increasingly ⁠⁠engaged in hostilities’ against Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
The United States Department of State has ordered the departure of nonemergency government employees and their family ⁠members from its mission in Saudi Arabia as attacks by the Iran-aligned Houthi movement on the kingdom have ramped up.

“Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly ⁠engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports ⁠and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a social media post on Wednesday.

“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority, and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them,” he added.

Pigott said that an earlier media report on US plans for the departure of some personnel and family members at US embassies across the Gulf was “inaccurate”.

Four US officials told the Reuters news agency that US missions in other Gulf states would also be ordering family members to leave.

The US had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months after many were pulled out when Tehran launched attacks on US facilities after the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February.

The latest withdrawals follow an escalation of fighting in ⁠Yemen, opening another front in the regional conflict triggered ⁠by the war. The conflict has snarled global energy trade and hurt Gulf economies.

The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by ‌the Houthis on Saudi Arabia after recent deadly strikes, including on Riyadh’s airport.

The embassy and a CIA station hosted there came under attack by drones in early March, ‌as ‌Iran began launching attacks across the region.

articles.title: Nigeria’s first Ebola case matches DR Congo strain, health officials say
articles.summary: The Bundibugyo strain outbreak is the DR Congo’s deadliest ever and has now reached West Africa for the first time.
articles.body:
Nigerian health officials say test results have confirmed the country’s first case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, which is behind a major outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), marking the disease’s first spread to West Africa in the current outbreak.

The case involves a woman who travelled from Uganda to the capital, Abuja, on October 3, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said.

She was tested for Ebola on October 19 after health officials learned she had recently travelled to Uganda, one of the countries affected by the current outbreak. Officials confirmed the positive result on Tuesday.

“We did three levels of tests, but all molecular. The strain was Bundibugyo,” Olajumoke Babatunde, director of the public health laboratory service at the NCDC, said on Wednesday.

The World Health Organization (WHO) also confirmed the strain, for which there is neither a vaccine nor a specific treatment.

An unnamed official told the AFP news agency that the woman is a diplomat whose condition has deteriorated into “multi-organ failure”.

Ayoade Alakija, a Nigerian physician who co-chairs a G7 committee for investment in global health, said that it had taken 12 days since the woman fell sick for her to be tested for Ebola, potentially exposing many other people to the infection.

Nigerian authorities have identified 44 contacts, most of them healthcare workers. They include the patient’s husband, a Swiss national, who lives with her in Abuja.

Officials are also tracing passengers who travelled with her from Uganda to Nigeria but do not believe she was symptomatic during the flight.

Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate told public broadcaster NTA that the woman was in isolation and receiving treatment.

In 2014, the first Nigerian case, detected in Lagos, raised fears the virus would spread rapidly, but it was brought under control within three months, resulting in 20 infections and eight deaths.

That epidemic killed more than 11,000 people across West Africa between late 2013 and 2016.

The WHO says Nigeria is the fifth country to detect the virus in the outbreak, which this past week widened across the continent, with Kenya in the east reporting nine cases since October 6.

Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Director-General Jean Kaseya said on X on Wednesday that the outbreak was “no longer one country’s fight”, and that he would hold a meeting of Africa’s health ministers next week to strengthen the cross-border response and review hospital capacity.

The DRC is the epicentre of the outbreak, its deadliest on record.

There have been more than 9,000 Ebola cases and more than 4,000 deaths there since mid-May.

articles.title: Pope Leo needs no further treatment after cancer surgery, doctors say
articles.summary: The 71-year-old leader of the Catholic Church has had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery.
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment for lung cancer after confirming the disease had not spread following recent surgery, the Vatican announced in a statement from doctors.

“A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the pope’s lead surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said Wednesday.

The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung surgically removed on October 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Leo was discharged from Rome’s Gemelli Polyclinic on Saturday, four days after his operation, and the Vatican said he would gradually resume his activities. On Wednesday, he returned to St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with pilgrims.

Additional treatment is generally offered in cases where follow-up testing finds signs that the cancer has spread, such as through the lymph nodes, or if other signs indicate that it might be particularly aggressive. Surgery often can be enough when tumours are caught very early, as the Catholic leader appears to have had, when the nodule was initially found during another unrelated exam.

In an interview with Vatican News on Saturday, Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, confirmed that the nodule was found by chance during routine abdominal examinations, and that the pope had not been experiencing any symptoms.

The pope carried on his official business while in the hospital, including a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin. He has appeared strong in two public appearances at the Vatican since his surgery: the traditional Sunday blessing from a window overlooking St Peter’s Square and Wednesday’s longer audience in the square, greeting the faithful from around the world.

“Thank you! Thank you for the support of your prayers,” Leo exclaimed to the audience.

It appears that the Catholic leader remains committed to his November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Leo’s lead surgeon told Vatican News that there was “no clinical reason” to prevent the trip, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and high-altitude stops.

articles.title: The 'trillion pound' oil fund the government believes Britain could have built
articles.summary: For the first time, the Treasury calculates how much the UK could have raised by investing North Sea proceeds.
articles.body:
After a half-century wait, the United Kingdom now has an oil fund.

Chancellor John Healey announced the creation of an Energy Wealth Fund at the Jackdaw gas approval announcement on Wednesday, with £2bn of funding diverted from the existing National Wealth Fund.

A selection of energy exporting countries, mainly in the Gulf, but also including Norway, over the years have amassed multi-trillion funds using oil and gas revenues to create epic national piggy banks.

It has been a long-standing debate in UK economic policy circles. If neighbouring Norway has amassed a $2.4tn war chest from the same North Sea, where exactly did the UK's sovereign wealth fund go?

It is an apposite question on the week when the national debt also hit £3tn for the first time.

"The proceeds of this oil and gas coming ashore now can be invested for the future generations," the chancellor said.

"If we had done this when North Sea oil was first discovered in the 1980s, we'd have a British Sovereign Wealth Fund now that would be worth probably a trillion pounds."

On Wednesday, for the first time, Treasury officials actually calculated how much that missing British fund could have been worth.

The trillion pound number comes from internal Treasury modelling. The assumption was that the UK's historical North Sea receipts of £200bn had been invested, with no withdrawals and grown at a rate comparable to Norway's.

"Norway demonstrates the power of long-term investment: the government wants to learn from that principle, rather than copy its model wholesale," one insider told me.

It was a "missed opportunity" which "had we systematically invested those receipts, we could have built a huge national asset for future generations", they said.

Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences

It is a giant "What if?" asked often by economists critical of the Margaret Thatcher era.

The peak oil revenues were, in their view, frittered away in pre-election tax cuts, which ended up being spent on 1980s garden conservatories.

Others might argue that the revenues under subsequent governments were squandered on wasteful government spending. It is worth noting that Norway's fund only began in earnest in 1996.

The idea of a lost oil fund has also featured in arguments from supporters of Scottish independence, and was suggested by some government advisers in the 1970s.

I have met some of the officials running Norway's fund. They are sometimes lambasted by ordinary Norwegians on the Oslo commuter trains who can all check the live value of the national fund.

Three percent of its value is drawn down each year to fund a fifth to a quarter of government budgets. The nation drew down on the fund during the coronavirus pandemic.

It is meant to help fund Norway's post oil economy and society, as indeed are some of the equivalent funds in the Gulf. It is a gift to the future.

While the UK government promises to divert new revenues into its new fund, it will be run rather differently. Norway's fund is obliged to invest abroad, and has grown hugely off the back off investments in US big tech. The UK plan is to create a fund that can invest domestically in green energy. It may struggle to match the performance.

UK energy tax revenues are also forecast to dwindle as North Sea production slows. The rate of slowing may now ease, with Jackdaw and extensions to existing fields. Critically Norway's state still controls its oil companies, also giving a share of their profits.

Two billion Norwegian Kroner was exactly the starting investment in Norway's fund 30 years ago. It is now worth over a thousand times that.

Nobody expects the Energy Wealth Fund's £2bn to be worth £2tn by 2056. The question is: what might have been, had a similar, far-sighted idea been adopted here in decades past?

How much gas could Jackdaw provide? And will it cut your energy bills?

articles.title: California mayor insists cash handout program will solve affordability challenges, but critics question cost
articles.summary: Alameda Mayor Marilyn Ezzy Ashcraft told Fox News Digital the city's $4.6 million guaranteed income pilot worked, but federal ARPA funds ran dry.
articles.body: A California mayor insisted that handing out monthly cash payments is an effective tool to combat the state's soaring cost of living, even as local leaders face steep hurdles in securing permanent taxpayer funding to keep guaranteed income programs alive. "I believe that guaranteed income programs like our Rise Up Alameda (RUA) pilot program are a valuable and effective tool to address the affordability crisis, based on the documented experiences of program participants," Alameda Mayor Marilyn Ezzy Ashcraft told Fox News Digital. "The average age of the 150 program participants was 49 years, with 26% being 62 years or older, and most participants were either employed or retired." Ashcraft’s comments follow the completion of Rise Up Alameda, the city's first-ever guaranteed income pilot project. City staff presented the program's final 24-month evaluation report to the Alameda City Council on Oct. 6. ALBUQUERQUE USES WEED TAX TO FUND 'NO-STRINGS-ATTACHED' GUARANTEED INCOME, SPARKING POLICY DEBATE According to city documents, the pilot aimed to "reduce economic instability for program participants, help to change local narratives and perceptions surrounding poverty and the provision of public benefits and help to support and inform the national discussion regarding public benefits and anti-poverty policies." The Alameda City Council previously allocated $4.6 million in federal pandemic relief funds from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) to finance the initiative, which provided 150 low-income households with $1,000 per month in no-strings-attached cash over two years. However, city notices confirm that because ARPA was a one-time federal allocation, the pilot has officially concluded, and the city has no plans or budget allocated for a permanent continuation. "As mayor, I believe our responsibility is to advance practical, compassionate and evidence-informed policies that help residents meet their basic needs, preserve their dignity and build a more stable future for themselves and their families," Ashcraft told Fox News Digital when asked whether she planned to implement a permanent program. BALTIMORE MAYOR BACKS BALLOT MEASURE CREATING TAXPAYER-FUNDED 'BABY FUND' FOR NEWBORN FAMILIES The faces behind the program Ashcraft highlighted several personal accounts of local residents who received monthly payments through the pilot. Among them was Andrea, a certified nursing assistant who used the funds to stay afloat following the death of her mother. The financial boost helped cover medical bills, rent, gas and Bay Area bridge tolls while allowing her to care for her father and ailing brother. Another participant, Dolores, a retiree in her 70s living in affordable senior housing after a 41-year career at AT&T, used the extra $1,000 a month to pay off credit card debt and build an emergency savings account. Other recipients included Haroon, a rideshare and transit driver; Julia, a woman with a disability who was able to buy new mattresses, groceries and a set of car tires after an eviction forced her to move in with her sister; and Tyronne, a Navy veteran and former truck driver at the decommissioned Alameda Naval Air Station who relied on the extra money to cover medical bills and stabilize his housing. While Ashcraft praised these personal outcomes, she acknowledged that direct cash payments are not a full remedy for California's economic pressures. "These stories demonstrate the value of direct, unrestricted cash in helping residents navigate financial hardship, maintain stability and improve their overall well-being," Ashcraft said. "While guaranteed income is not a stand-alone solution to the affordability crisis, programs like Rise Up Alameda can provide meaningful support as we pursue longer-term solutions to the high cost of housing, health care, transportation and other basic needs." GUARANTEED INCOME PROGRAM TARGETS LOW-INCOME HOMES LED BY BLACK MOMS AS CASH HANDOUTS SURGE NATIONWIDE How will municipalities fund these programs? Alameda's program underscores a funding challenge local governments face across the nation regarding how to sustain guaranteed income pilot programs now that temporary federal pandemic relief funding is ending. Many local guaranteed income pilots were underwritten by temporary pandemic-era ARPA allocations. With federal deadlines requiring municipalities to spend remaining relief funds, mayors and advocacy groups are searching for ways to convert short-term experiments into permanent, taxpayer-funded government programs. A major organization advocating for guaranteed income is the Economic Security Project (ESP). Founded in 2016 by a network of entrepreneurs, activists and researchers, ESP has helped support more than 100 guaranteed income pilots nationwide. California leads the country with more than 60 pilot launches. ESP has urged governments to consider taxpayer-funded measures to establish permanent minimum-income guarantees. When asked by Fox News Digital whether local pilots are transitioning into permanent public policies, ESP indicated that multiple municipalities are actively working on legislative proposals. "We can say, however, that there’s an active and growing movement for cash in hundreds of communities across the country," Shafeka Hashash, director of cash initiatives at the Economic Security Project, told Fox News Digital. "We regularly take calls from some of the 1,500 members of the Guaranteed Income Community of Practice — researchers, nonprofits, local government officials and community leaders all interested in bringing cash to their neighborhoods," Hashash added. "We just can’t announce any pilots or policies before the localities do." MICHIGAN LAWMAKER MOVES TO SHUT DOWN 'GUARDRAIL-FREE' CASH HANDOUT PROGRAM FOR NEW MOTHERS One pilot program has become permanent in Cook County, Illinois. To sustain the initiative without federal aid, the Cook County Board of Commissioners approved $7.5 million for guaranteed income in the county budget, signaling a shift toward long-term local funding. Republican state officials and conservative policy groups have sought to block guaranteed income programs. Critics argue unconditional handouts discourage work, increase dependence on government assistance and misuse taxpayer funds. "The affordability crisis is hitting Americans across backgrounds, geographies and party lines, and it's imperative that state and federal leaders adopt a solutions-focused approach," Mayors for Guaranteed Income founder Michael Tubbs told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Banning policies that have proven effective at the local level is not only undemocratic, it is incredibly counterproductive to solving the key problem facing American families," he added. "We should be unlocking innovation at the local level to boost economic security, stabilize households and restore faith in the American dream."

articles.title: Peter Thiel breaks with Trump over Iran war: ‘We should not have done it’
articles.summary: The remarks from an early tech-world supporter of the president are his most explicit on the war dividing Republicans.
articles.body:
Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel said he's skeptical of the U.S. war with Iran and does not believe the United States should have launched it, putting the major Republican donor at odds with President Donald Trump over one of the administration's defining foreign policy decisions.

Thiel's remarks, delivered on Oct. 12 at a private event, are his most explicit statements to be revealed publicly about the war with Iran and come less than two weeks before the midterm elections in which Trump's party is grasping to maintain power in Congress. The audio of Thiel's comments was obtained by Decoded by POLITICO from a lecture earlier this month.

"I'm skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it," Thiel said. "There were a lot of mistakes that were made."

Thiel added, "Maybe we don't have the hard power. Maybe we're going to lose the soft power war."

In the full lecture, Thiel made clear his strong opposition to neoconservatives and Middle East wars. Despite his criticism of the Iran war, Thiel highlighted his continued support of Trump and suggested he wanted to protect the president.

Still, Thiel's break over the war represents one of the most important examples to date of a fierce Trump ally sharing deep concerns about the conflict.

The comments were part of Thiel's lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has documented since their start this fall . In the latest lecture, Thiel issued extensive warnings about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, drawing on comments from Bush-era figures Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney.

"I read the Cheney family's Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late," Thiel said. "And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran."

Thiel also discusses meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, after the Oct. 7 attack, where he said he asked the leader about his plans in Gaza. Thiel said Netanyahu told him, "I can't just Dresdenize it," referring to the Allied bombing of the German city of Dresden during World War II that killed roughly 25,000 people.

The first big tech investor to back Trump in 2016, and then have a high-profile speaking role at the Republican National Convention that year, Thiel was also the biggest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance's Senate campaign in 2022. POLITICO reported in March that Vance was "skeptical" of the U.S. striking Iran in the lead-up to the beginning of the war.

Representatives for Thiel and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

CORRECTION: An earlier version of this report misstated Benjamin Netanyahu's title.

articles.title: Brazilian tourist killed by piece of roof blown off Frank Lloyd Wright's winter home in Arizona
articles.summary: Witnesses said Rogério Renato Mateucci, 55, died instantly. He was visiting the U.S. to attend an international program at Arizona State University, the Brazilian university he worked for said.
articles.body: SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. — The Arizona desert home of famed architect Frank Lloyd Wright remained temporarily closed to the public Wednesday after part of a roof blew off in high winds, killing a visitor from Brazil who was touring the historic property last week. Witnesses say Rogério Renato Mateucci, 55, was struck in the head and died instantly Friday, according to police in Scottsdale, east of Phoenix. He was killed by a piece of plastic glass roofing, said Sgt. Allison Sempsis, a police spokesperson. Wind gusts of up to 38 mph were recorded at the Scottsdale Airport that day, according to the National Weather Service. The 1937 home and surrounding compound, called Taliesin West, have low-slung roofs and rock walls that appear to blend into the surrounding desert. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage site, the property draws up to 100,000 visitors a year, according to the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation, its owner. It served as Wright's winter home, as well as a “desert laboratory” for his students. The foundation said in a statement following Mateucci's death that the property was closed to the public “until further notice.” A foundation spokesperson did not respond to an email Wednesday asking when tours would resume. Mateucci worked as the senior administrator at the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, located in the Brazilian city of Curitiba. In a statement, the school said he was its rector and a lay member of the Catholic order of Marist priests and brothers. He was from the city of São Paulo. The school said Mateucci was visiting the U.S. to attend an international program at Arizona State University. Wright's foundation offered its condolences Saturday, saying on social media that it wouldn’t comment further while there’s an active police investigation. Sempsis said the police investigation doesn’t prevent the site from reopening.

articles.title: Teacher who survived Bend shooting tried to close door, ‘but the shooter was already there’
articles.summary: Becky Drury was shot and seriously wounded by the gunman, who killed three children and another teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Oregon.
articles.body: A teacher who was shot by a teenage gunman in a Bend, Oregon, elementary school last week said she saw the attacker and tried to shut the classroom door, “but the shooter was already there.” Becky Drury said she was shot at close range in the rampage at Silver Rail Elementary School on Thursday. “Lying on the floor, I saw that my left hand was almost completely severed from the gunshot, and my other arm was also severely injured,” Drury said in a statement Wednesday. “I could not get up, defend myself, or protect anyone else,” she said. “So, I did the only thing I could do, which was to pretend to be dead in the hope he would not shoot me again.” Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher were killed in the attack, which began around 1 p.m., officials said. The gunman was fatally shot by a bystander who saw him fire at a truck and enter the school, police have said. The bystander followed the 16-year-old gunman and shot him as another teacher was wrestling with him over the weapon, according to police. The motive remained under investigation Wednesday. Investigators are looking into whether the shooter viewed any extremist material online, including material associated with “nihilistic violent extremism,” also known as NVE, two senior law enforcement officials briefed on the investigation told NBC News. The gun was purchased legally, Bend police said in a statement Wednesday. Police have said that it was a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun and that the shooter used birdshot, buckshot and slugs. Police have not said who purchased the gun. Two senior law enforcement officials previously told NBC News that the shooter’s mother bought it in August, around the time of his birthday. “Bend Police detectives continue this complex investigation. They have served search warrants at the shooting suspect’s home, as well as on his electronic devices and his social media accounts on a variety of platforms,” police said in a statement Wednesday. “That work continues, and it takes time,” the police department said. Students in the greater Bend-La Pine Schools district returned to class Wednesday, although not at Silver Rail Elementary, where the shooting occurred. “Through heartfelt artwork and messages of love, they are making sure every student who walks through the doors knows they are cared for, supported and loved,” the district said Tuesday as it prepared to welcome most students back. Authorities have publicly identified two of the victims who were killed, 5-year-old Rhoam Summer and teacher Megan Lambert. Drury, the wounded teacher, said in her statement that she heard a noise last week and went to investigate. “Here is what I remember: Once I realized something was happening outside, I ran to see what was going on,” she said. “I then saw the shooter and immediately ran back into the classroom. I turned to shut the door behind me, but the shooter was already there,” she said. Drury said that there was nothing more she could have done and that “I was shot before I had any chance to act.” “What happened in that classroom was unimaginable, and like so many in this community, my heart is broken for everyone affected by this tragedy,” she said. “My thoughts are with those who were hurt, those we lost, their families, our school, and the Bend community,” she said. “I am truly grateful for the kindness and support we have received as we face the difficult days ahead together.”

Three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, were killed in the Oct. 13 attack. Mathieu Lewis-Rolland / Getty

articles.title: US accuses Canada of election interference ahead of midterms
articles.summary: Washington cites Canadian tariffs, political meetings and anti-Trump ads as evidence of attempted election interference.
articles.body:
The United States has accused Canadian politicians of trying to influence its midterm elections, pointing to Canada’s efforts to push back against President Donald Trump’s tariff campaign.

In a fact sheet released on Wednesday, the US embassy accused Canada of being dismissive of its allegations of election interference.

“The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances,” the fact sheet reads.

The two countries have been locked in a trade war since the start of Trump’s second term in 2025, with Canada responding to US tariffs with import taxes of its own.

But the US embassy identified public statements about the tariffs as being attempts to sway the November 3 midterm election.

Among the politicians singled out in the fact sheet was Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly. The fact sheet pointed to comments Joly made in August about responding to Trump’s tariffs.

“We’re also targeting products that will target states in the US. And so we’re being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” Joly said at the time.

The embassy also took issue with Joly’s meetings with Democratic officials in Boston and Chicago in September. When asked by a reporter what she thought might happen with regard to tariffs if Democrats won the midterms, she said, “That’s exactly why I’m meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates.”

Joly has rejected the suggestion that her actions could amount to interference, saying Canada would never meddle in US elections. She said her meetings with US politicians, both Democratic and Republican, were about building Canada’s economy.

“Fundamentally, what I’ve done in the US is to attract investments,” she told reporters on October 14.

The embassy also pointed to Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s calls for retaliatory measures on US products, as well as his government’s advertising campaign against Trump’s tariffs, launched last year.

The campaign, which featured clips of former US President Ronald Reagan criticising tariffs in a 1987 radio address, prompted Trump to call off trade talks with Canada in October 2025.

While the embassy laid out several examples of Canadian officials trying to influence US trade policy, it didn’t explain how those efforts amounted to interference.

Other instances of alleged election interference included Liberal MP Anthony Housefather saying he had campaigned in Florida on behalf of Democratic Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz, ahead of her primary election in August.

The fact sheet also accused individual Canadians of illegally participating in US elections, naming 11 people who had been charged or sentenced for voting between 2012 and 2024.

The sheet did not, however, present any evidence linking those citizens to a Canadian government effort to involve itself in US elections.

“All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence U.S. elections in any way,” the US embassy’s statement said. “Americans decide America’s elections.”

The fact sheet comes a week after US Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra said Washington was closely watching Canada for signs of interference ahead of the midterms.

“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it and if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond to it,” Hoekstra said in a podcast interview on The Really Big Show, according to The Canadian Press.

The US and Canada have long been allies, but relations have frayed since Trump returned to office.

Not only has the Republican leader triggered a trade war with Canada, but he has also repeatedly threatened to make Canada a 51st state.

There have also been reports that separatist leaders from Alberta had sought support from Trump administration officials ahead of a failed referendum on the province’s independence this week.

Ahead of Monday’s provincial vote, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed concerns about potential US interference in the referendum, saying Canada expected foreign governments to stay out of its elections.

“Our expectation is, to be absolutely clear, on foreign governments, United States included, is we don’t get ourselves involved in their elections, they don’t get themselves involved in our elections,” he told Global News.

Al Jazeera has reached out to the Prime Minister’s Office and Global Affairs Canada for comment, as well as the office of Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Industry Minister Joly.

articles.title: Troca de gêmeos no batizado: bebê recebe sacramento duas vezes | G1
articles.standfirst: Mãe conta que a família já confundia os bebês em casa por causa da semelhança entre eles; João Felipe acabou sendo batizado duas vezes após ser levado à pia batismal no lugar do irmão Caio Henrique.
articles.summary: Após confusão da família em Guaratinguetá, o pequeno João Felipe foi levado à pia batismal no lugar do irmão e acabou recebendo o sacramento duas vezes.
articles.body:
Uma cena inusitada marcou o batizado de gêmeos idênticos na comunidade Santa Teresinha, em Guaratinguetá , no interior de SP. O padre Paulo Roberto da Silva, da Paróquia Nossa Senhora de Fátima, acabou batizando um dos bebês duas vezes após confundi-lo com o irmão.

Segundo o padre, os bebês eram muito parecidos, tinham personalidade semelhante e usavam roupas iguais. Para evitar a troca, ele decidiu chamar os irmãos separadamente.

Mesmo com o cuidado, a troca aconteceu. Depois de derramar a água sobre a cabeça do bebê e pronunciar o nome de Caio Henrique, o padre foi avisado de que a criança era, na verdade, João Felipe.

“Eu falei: ‘Meu Deus, tem que trazer o certo, porque eu tenho que batizar com o nome certo, a pessoa certa com o nome certo’”, relembrou.

A família levou Caio até a pia batismal, onde ele recebeu o sacramento. Em seguida, João também foi batizado. O episódio aconteceu em 12 de setembro e foi contado pela mãe dos bebês nas redes sociais (leia mais abaixo).

Confusão durante batizado de gêmeos fez um dos bebês receber o sacramento duas vezes em Guaratinguetá (SP). — Foto: Renata D’andrea Fotografia/Reprodução

Cansaço e troca de colo contribuíram para a confusão

A mãe dos gêmeos e vice-diretora de escola, Ana Luísa de Almeida Prado Silva, contou ao g1 que a confusão começou ainda em casa. A família acordou cedo para se preparar para a cerimônia, marcada para as 10h, e os bebês vestiam roupas iguais - veja vídeo acima.

“Quando colocou as duas roupas iguais, a gente já não sabia mais quem que era quem”, contou.

Segundo Ana Luísa, a única diferença física que ajudava a identificar os meninos era uma pequena mancha no olho de Caio. Na correria da preparação, porém, nem isso foi suficiente para evitar a troca.

A família chegou à igreja pouco antes do início da cerimônia. Enquanto aguardavam, os bebês passaram de colo em colo entre os pais e os familiares.

Durante o batizado, o padre anunciou que chamaria um dos gêmeos por vez. Quando chamou Caio, uma prima da mãe se levantou com João, enquanto Ana Luísa permaneceu com o bebê correto no colo.

“Na hora em que o padre chamou, por um momento de desatenção nosso, a gente não pensou nisso. Do jeito que o padre chamou os gêmeos, a minha prima foi e já começou a deitar o João. E eu esqueci que eu estava com o Caio”, relembrou.

A mãe percebeu o engano quando ouviu o padre pronunciar o nome de Caio durante o batismo. “Eu virei para o meu marido e falei: ‘Amor, ele está batizando o bebê errado. O Caio é esse daqui que está no meu colo, aquele ali é o João’”, contou.

Apesar da vergonha inicial, o casal decidiu avisar o padre. O sacerdote interrompeu o momento para corrigir a troca, e a situação acabou provocando risadas entre eles.

Momento em que a família percebe troca de gêmeos durante batizado. — Foto: Renata D’andrea Fotografia/Reprodução

O padre disse que ficou preocupado em corrigir a confusão, mas que o clima descontraído ajudou a tornar o episódio uma lembrança especial.Depois da cerimônia, ele também fez uma piada sobre o futuro de João, que havia recebido o sacramento duas vezes.

“João, se Deus quiser, vai ser padre, porque você foi batizado duas vezes”, contou.

Segundo o padre, a família é conhecida e querida pela comunidade. Ele também destacou que os bebês estavam tranquilos durante a celebração e não choraram, o que tornou ainda mais difícil perceber a troca.

Depois de três anos sem nenhuma reposição, o Executivo Municipal sancionou a Lei nº 3293, de 14 de outubro, que concede reajuste anual sobre os vencimentos básicos dos servidores públicos efetivos e contratados da Administração Pública Municipal Direta e Indireta do Município.

Publicada na Edição nº 2026 do Jornal Oficial, o reajuste atende os termos do art.37, X, da Constituição Federal e será de 4,22% referente à variação do índice IPCA (Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor Amplo), acumulada nos últimos 12 meses, aplicando-se sobre os vencimentos básicos já a partir do pagamento deste mês.

De acordo com o prefeito Carlos Augusto Balthazar, essa conquista faz parte da política de valorização do servidor. “Quando assumimos a Prefeitura no ano passado, encontramos uma folha salarial com percentual acima do limite permitido por Lei. Tivemos que adequar a folha de pagamento, com muita responsabilidade, e investir em ações que garantiram a melhoria na arrecadação da receita própria. Já nesse segundo ano de governo, conseguimos conceder esse direito importante do servidor. Vamos continuar trabalhando para que possamos, nos próximos anos, reparar as perdas salariais e garantir outros benefícios para os servidores”, declarou o prefeito.

AQUECIMENTO NA ECONOMIA – Com o reajuste, a economia local também será beneficiada, tendo em vista que, com o aumento salarial, o servidor do Município acaba investindo mais no comércio local. “Sabemos que os servidores compram nos nossos mercados, padarias e comércio da Cidade em geral. Isso acaba fortalecendo a nossa economia e gerando mais empregos também”, lembrou o prefeito Carlos Augusto.

articles.title: Três diagnósticos de câncer e uma síndrome rara: veja história  | G1
articles.standfirst: Auxiliar de farmácia enfrentou três diagnósticos de câncer ao longo da vida por causa de uma alteração genética hereditária. Hoje, segue um protocolo rigoroso de acompanhamento e não teve novos tumores detectados.
articles.summary: Auxiliar de farmácia enfrentou três diagnósticos de câncer ao longo da vida por causa de uma alteração genética hereditária. Hoje, segue um protocolo rigoroso de acompanhamento e não teve novos tumores detectados.
articles.body:
Uma alteração genética herdada marcou a vida da auxiliar de farmácia Andréa Domingues desde a infância. Aos 6 anos, ela recebeu o primeiro diagnóstico de câncer e precisou enfrentar a doença novamente, aos 7 e 12. A sequência de tumores acabou levando à descoberta de uma condição rara, a síndrome de Li-Fraumeni, que aumenta significativamente o risco de diversos tipos de câncer ao longo da vida.

"A primeira vez que eu tive o câncer, eu tinha 6 anos. Foi um câncer de suprarrenal, ele pesou 3 quilos", relembra. "Depois ele apareceu no rim, fiz a cirurgia e retirei o rim esquerdo. Quando eu tinha 12 anos, ele apareceu novamente no pulmão e aí eu tirei um terço do pulmão direito."

A história de Andréa ilustra os desafios enfrentados por pessoas que convivem com a síndrome de Li-Fraumeni, uma alteração hereditária causada por mutações no gene TP53, conhecido pelos especialistas como o "guardião dos genes". Quando esse mecanismo de proteção falha, o organismo perde parte da capacidade de impedir o crescimento desordenado de células tumorais.

'Tive câncer aos 6 anos, aos 7 e novamente aos 12': história de uma paciente com síndrome genética rara — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

Diagnóstico precoce e vigilância constante

Desde os episódios de câncer na infância e adolescência, Andréa passou a seguir uma rotina rigorosa de monitoramento. O acompanhamento inclui exames periódicos capazes de identificar eventuais tumores ainda em estágios iniciais.

Ressonâncias anuais, ultrassonografias e exames de saguem fazem parte da rotina de tratamentos. Desde que iniciou o protocolo, nenhum novo turmo foi detectado.

Segundo especialistas que acompanham pacientes com a síndrome, o rastreamento frequente é uma das principais ferramentas para aumentar a sobrevida. A recomendação é que os exames sejam realizados nos intervalos definidos pelos protocolos médicos, mesmo na ausência de sintomas.

"Aqueles que aderem ao rastreamento, que aceitam fazer os exames da forma que é preconizado, viveram mais do que quem não aceitou e deixou para fazer exames só quando sentiu algum sintoma que já era um tumor", afirma uma das especialistas ouvidas pela reportagem.

O resultado desse acompanhamento rigoroso aparece nos exames de Andréa: desde que iniciou o protocolo de vigilância, nenhum novo tumor foi detectado.

A síndrome de Li-Fraumeni está associada a um risco aumentado de câncer, mas especialistas destacam que o diagnóstico não representa uma certeza de que a doença irá surgir.

"Você não herda câncer e você não herda uma certeza. Você herda um risco", explica a médica Maria Isabel, que há mais de três décadas estuda a síndrome.

A condição ganhou atenção especial no Brasil porque uma mutação específica é encontrada com frequência maior do que em outros países, especialmente nas regiões Sul e Sudeste. Pesquisadores investigam como essa alteração genética se espalhou ao longo das gerações e tentam dimensionar seu impacto na população brasileira.

Apesar de o Sistema Único de Saúde (SUS) oferecer serviços especializados para testagem genética e acompanhamento em alguns centros de referência, muitos pacientes ainda não sabem que carregam a mutação.

Especialistas defendem que perguntas simples sobre histórico familiar de câncer durante atendimentos nas unidades básicas de saúde podem ajudar a identificar pessoas com maior risco e encaminhá-las para avaliação especializada.

Para a médica Maria Isabel, o conhecimento sobre a síndrome permite transformar a forma de lidar com a própria saúde. Em vez de viver à espera da doença, ela aposta na prevenção e no diagnóstico precoce.

"'A ideia que você tem uma síndrome não é para ser um peso, é para ser uma grande oportunidade para a gente poder diagnosticar precocemente o câncer e prevenir", ressalta.

articles.title: One killed, 8 injured in Saudi airport attack amid US order for diplomats to leave
articles.summary: A Saudi resident was killed and eight others were injured when an attack struck King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, late on
articles.body: A Saudi resident was killed and eight others were injured when an attack struck King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, eastern Saudi Arabia, late on Wednesday, according to the country's Civil Aviation Authority.The airport, located on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar, also sustained material damage, the authority said early on Thursday. Flightradar24, a global flight-tracking service, said on X that aircraft were being diverted away from the airport following the incident.Saudi authorities have not identified those responsible for the attack or disclosed further details. The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have also not commented on the incident.Saudi Arabia reports drone interceptionsThe attack comes amid a wider series of strikes targeting Saudi Arabia, including attacks on airports, shipping routes and energy infrastructure. The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted four drone attacks in the kingdom's eastern region.King Fahd International Airport has previously been targeted during waves of Houthi missile and projectile attacks on major Saudi airports.The latest incident follows another deadly attack in the country's south-east. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said debris from a drone intercepted by the country's defences killed two people and injured two others at an oil field operated by Aramco.The two people killed were nationals of Nepal and the Philippines, while the injured were from Pakistan and India, the ministry said.US orders diplomats to leaveThe United States ordered some of its diplomats and the family members of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia late on Wednesday. The move followed a series of deadly attacks attributed to Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels and growing concerns that the conflict could escalate further.The latest violence has raised concerns about the security of Saudi Arabia's critical infrastructure, particularly its oil facilities and transport hubs.Last month, debris from an intercepted Houthi drone killed a Yemeni resident in Saudi Arabia. articles.title: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
articles.summary: The warning to US officials comes as at least three people die in the latest strikes at an airport and an oil field.
articles.body:
The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.

Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.

The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.

"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.

"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.

The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".

In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.

No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.

The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.

An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: Colorado couple spent nearly three years building an earth home from 1,500 recycled tyres and mud; the four-bedroom property is now listed for $1.3 million
articles.summary: A mud home built with tyres in Colorado has come to market, offering buyers a rare chance to own a sustainable earth home made from recycled materials.
articles.body: A mud home built with tyres in Colorado has come to market, offering buyers a rare chance to own a sustainable earth home made from recycled materials. Set in the Black Forest area of Colorado Springs, this eco-friendly property was largely built by its owners with their own hands, and it now carries a $1.3 million price tag. For anyone searching for self-sustaining homes or unique properties in Colorado, it is a genuine standout. Read on to discover how it was built, how it stays comfortable, what its interiors and grounds offer, and why nature lovers are its target buyers.How the sellers hand-crafted a self-sustaining Black Forest earth home, doing 90 per cent of the work themselvesTucked away on a lush, green parcel in Colorado Springs' Black Forest, the residence was hand-crafted in 1997 from more than 1,500 recycled tyres, mud, aluminium cans and glass bottles. Construction took the sellers nearly three years, and the listing agent, Jennifer Browne of The Fletcher Team & Associates, told Realtor that they did 90 per cent of the work themselves. She described the project as a strong labour of love. More than two decades on, the sellers are ready to hand the home to a buyer seeking a self-sustaining dwelling designed for comfort.How passive and active solar design holds the earth home at 65 degrees all year, with five skylightsThe house was designed to maintain 65 degrees Fahrenheit (about 18 degrees Celsius) inside all year round, Browne told the publication, and all of its windows have rain sensors so that they can be opened and closed. According to the listing, the home's energy efficiency comes from passive and active solar design, a rubber membrane roof and a stucco exterior, along with slanted windows lining the front of the house and five skylights that provide natural light.Custom mosaics, 12 mandalas, a poured-earth floor, curved rooms and private observatories shape the interiorNatural materials run throughout the design, even in the decorative elements. The four-bedroom house has a 4,461-square-foot (about 414 square metres) open floor plan, with curved rooms that appear to merge with the world around them. Custom mosaics, 12 mandalas and an entry piece that works as a water feature decorate the interior, while exposed wood ceilings and enormous beams give the living spaces a treehouse-like feel. The floor is poured earth. Built-in seating, kiva fireplaces and a split kitchen with a prep area, pantry and dining space complete the main living areas. The primary suite adds dual closets, a spa-inspired bathroom with a heat-retaining tub built with stones, and a walk-out patio, while two nonconforming bedrooms have exclusive access to private observatories.Land, outbuildings and a $1.3 million asking price aimed at buyers who want to feel connected to natureThe 6.81-acre (about 2.76-hectare) parcel offers ample room for expansion or the creation of a compound-style estate. At present, it holds a two-car garage, cross-fenced acreage designed for horses, a 23-stall barn with hay storage, a heated tack shed with water, storage outbuildings, a fenced dog area and a pond. The home came to market at $1,299,900. Browne told Realtor that the next buyer will be someone who wants to feel connected to nature and more a part of the earth, although she added that the property could just as easily serve as a primary or secondary residence, a rental or a retreat, and could appeal to investors as well as those seeking a sustainable home.You use AI every day. articles.body: During a podcast interview Wednesday, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton criticized a video from actor Matthew McConaughey encouraging voters to consider independent candidates. On Sunday, McConaughey took to social media and challenged the long-held notion that voting for an independent candidate is a wasted vote, arguing that just a handful of independent lawmakers could dramatically shift the balance of power in Washington. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS THE HOUSE FALLS, THE SENATE STAYS IN PLAY Liberal journalist Kara Swisher shared the video with Clinton on their new podcast "High Stakes," remarking that she didn't think McConaughey articulated the appeal of independent candidates well enough for viewers. Clinton went further and criticized McConaughey for potentially complicating the Democratic Party's efforts to push back against President Donald Trump in the midterm elections. "I think it's really unfortunate that somebody who's such a great actor with such a reach would be two weeks before a midterm that is aimed at stopping Trump's corruption, impunity and extreme damage to the country would suggest that any independent candidate is really a better choice," Clinton said. HILLARY CLINTON ISSUES ENDORSEMENT IN US MIDTERM ELECTIONS "Right now, we have a broad range of Democrats running, and Democrats are representing, I think, every kind of American in these elections," she continued. articles.title: Ilhan Omar believes Trump raid on home was meant to 'intimidate and scare people' from voting
articles.summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., claimed the raid on her D.C. home was designed to intimidate voters ahead of midterm elections and appease Trump supporters.
articles.body: Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., told MS NOW Wednesday night that she believes the raid on her home was to "intimidate and scare people" away from voting in the midterm elections. Omar's home in Washington, D.C., was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) last Monday in connection to an investigation into potential immigration fraud. Authorities are probing whether Omar or her father lied on paperwork that helped her gain citizenship. Border czar Tom Homan has said that if the allegations are proven, Omar could be denaturalized. Omar, who has largely avoided public scrutiny since the raid, gave her first interview on the subject on "All In with Chris Hayes" and suggested that the decision to investigate her was a last-ditch effort by President Donald Trump to appeal to right-wing influencers. DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS "I think they were like starting to lose faith that these were empty promises, and they had to do something, I believe, to say, 'Hey, look, we raided her house. You know, now you can feel comfortable that we are doing something,'" Omar said. "I think ... whether it’s Metro Surge, whether it is the voter rolls that they’re looking at, whether it’s the door knocks that you just spoke of, that is all to show these people that they’re doing something and to save face." "Because they made this huge promise that there was somehow this massive ... sort of undocumented people that were voting in American elections and that there is something that they need to go and fix." "And so they, you know, they’re going to try to gin up this sort of frenzy," she added. "And, I think ultimately their goal is to intimidate and scare people from wanting to participate and vote." SOMALIS IN MINNESOTA UNLEASH FURY ON TRUMP AFTER FEDS RAID ILHAN OMAR'S DC HOME Despite that, Omar insisted that the raid had likely inspired people to vote in spite of the president. "As I was driving up here today, we were getting calls that people, you know, are just like, there’s a massive line at early voting sites. And a lot of our staff that are, you know, helping people drive to go vote are saying, you know, ‘We don’t have the capacity to keep up with the requests that we’re getting of people who need assistance to get to the early voting site.’ I think it’s doing the opposite," Omar said. Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment but did not immediately receive a response. ILHAN OMAR'S HUSBAND SNAPS OVER RUMORS SHE FLED US AFTER FEDERAL IMMIGRATION FRAUD RAID Prior to Tuesday night via a campaign video, Omar had not been seen publicly since before the raid on her home, which was first reported by Fox News Digital last week. Her husband, Tim Mynett, has been seen outside the residence walking their dog. Additionally, Fox News Digital has spotted a campaign aide bringing in food and both of her daughters arriving at the home two days apart. Trump warned Tuesday from the Oval Office that Omar could be jailed if the allegations against her are true. "Well, she could be. She could also go to jail," Trump said. "You know, they keep talking about deportation. No, she could go to jail." articles.title: Louisiana doctors lost their bad-faith case against AIG after a $16.1 million hurricane damage appraisal; a court upheld the jury’s verdict over the insurer’s earlier $6.7 million repair dispute
articles.summary: A Louisiana couple’s $16.1 million hurricane damage appraisal did not help them overturn a jury verdict in an insurance dispute.
articles.body: A Louisiana couple’s $16.1 million hurricane damage appraisal did not help them overturn a jury verdict in an insurance dispute. Raja and Gayathri Talluri, doctors who own a 25,000-square-foot home in Thibodaux, Louisiana, sued AIG Property Casualty over its refusal to pay their full $6.7 million repair estimate after Hurricane Ida damaged their property in August 2021. Although an appraisal later set the loss at $16,126,268, AIG paid the award in full. The couple’s remaining claim concerned whether the insurer had acted in bad faith by refusing to pay the full estimate submitted by ATA Loss Consulting. On February 10, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit upheld the jury’s verdict. The ruling highlights how insurance disputes can hinge on statutory deadlines and evidence of bad faith, even when later appraisals establish substantially higher damage estimates.Hurricane Ida damage sparks dispute over repair costs The Talluris’ home featured imported décor, including flooring from Nepal and roofing tiles from Colombia. Before AIG inspected the property, the couple hired Precision Construction & Roofing to tarp the roof for $86,404. AIG’s independent adjuster, White, inspected the home on September 24, 2021. His report two days later estimated restoration costs at more than $7 million but recommended that AIG withhold payment until an engineer and building consultant assisted with the claim. Three days after the inspection, the Talluris sent a demand letter seeking policy limits, roof-tarping costs and funds to replace the roof. On October 1, AIG denied the full claim but paid $106,404 for tarping and immediate needs.After further inspections, AIG’s building consultant, J.S. Held, initially estimated repairs at $359,479.21. AIG paid $309,479.21 after deducting the policy’s $50,000 deductible. The insurer later increased its estimate and made additional payments. On November 11, 2021, the Talluris submitted an ATA Loss Consulting estimate of $6,713,922.27, alongside an engineering report from Structural Alliance. AIG disputed parts of the estimate, particularly the proposed roof replacement. The roofing dispute involved replacing Santa Fe tiles with Ludowici tiles at an additional $8,000 per roofing square, equivalent to 100 square feet. At trial, AIG adjuster Eklund compared the proposal to “going from a Camry to a Rolls Royce.” AIG also disputed claimed water intrusion in the ballroom.Appraisal sets the loss at $16.1 million In February 2022, AIG invoked the policy’s appraisal process to resolve the remaining disputed damage. Each side appointed an appraiser, and the two selected an umpire after failing to agree on the loss amount. The Talluris’ appraiser, Irwin, inspected the property and prepared a valuation supported by 74 documents. On October 13, 2022, the umpire issued an award of $16,126,268.AIG paid approximately $10 million on November 9, excluding amounts already paid and additional living expenses and guaranteed rebuilding costs payable as incurred. It subsequently paid those expenses when the Talluris incurred them, satisfying the appraisal award in full. The couple sued in January 2023, alleging breach of contract and bad faith under Louisiana law. The district court granted partial summary judgment to AIG, finding that the insurer had paid all other amounts, including the appraisal award, within the required deadlines. The only issue left for trial was whether AIG acted in bad faith by refusing to pay the full ATA estimate.Why the Fifth Circuit upheld the jury’s verdict Before trial, the district court excluded the appraisal award and Irwin’s testimony about his valuation of the damage. The jury could still hear his observations of the property and his criticism of AIG’s estimates, as well as evidence about the appraisal process. The jury found that the Talluris had not proved AIG received satisfactory proof of loss and then failed to pay within Louisiana’s statutory 30-day period. Under the verdict form’s instructions, it did not need to decide whether AIG’s conduct was arbitrary or without probable cause.On appeal, the Talluris argued that excluding the appraisal amount and Irwin’s valuation testimony had prejudiced their case. AIG challenged whether the couple had preserved their objection to excluding the award amount. The Fifth Circuit rejected that argument, assumed without deciding that the exclusion was erroneous, and found any error harmless. The court reasoned that AIG did not know the final appraisal amount when it refused to pay the full ATA estimate months earlier. It also found Irwin’s excluded valuation cumulative of evidence the jury had already heard. Because the jury had found the first two elements of the bad-faith claim unproved, the appraisal award was unlikely to change the outcome. The three-judge panel of Circuit Judges Barksdale, Willett and Duncan affirmed the judgment in Talluri v. AIG Property Casualty, docket No. 24-30744, on appeal from the US District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, case No. 2:23-CV-377. The opinion was unpublished and is generally non-precedential under Fifth Circuit Rule 47.5.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
