articles.title: Drones fall, strikes stall: How Musk's Starshield curbs hit Zelenskyy’s war against Russia
articles.summary: A disruption in the US military satellite internet service Starshield caused Ukrainian drones worth more than $1 million to fall from the sky and forced
articles.body: A disruption in the US military satellite internet service Starshield caused Ukrainian drones worth more than $1 million to fall from the sky and forced troops to halt almost all operations for three days, The New York Times reported, citing Ukrainian military commanders.A senior Ukrainian commander, identified only by his first name, Oleh, said dozens of armed drones were heading towards Russian military targets last week when their video feeds suddenly went fuzzy. The drones had lost their connection to ground-based pilots through Starshield, a Pentagon-funded satellite internet service, he said.Many of the drones crashed, costing his units more than $1 million worth of weaponry, according to the report.The development comes days after Donald Trump’s reported engagement with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin over efforts to end the war in Ukraine. The MAGA supremo also recently eased sanctions on Russian oil.Oleh said the disruption forced his units to suspend almost all operations for the next three days, including strikes on Russian command posts and fuel hubs. Such attacks help protect Ukrainian troops on the front lines and slow Russian advances, he said.The reported disruptions have added to the growing tensions between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump. Ukrainian troops said connectivity had improved after a week, but problems persisted.The Trump administration has issued mixed statements on the issue, denying that any changes were made to satellite internet services in Ukraine while also saying that service had been restored.Ukrainian officials fear the disruptions were ordered to punish Kyiv for attacks on Russian oil refineries and pressure it into making concessions in the war. Ukraine has also reported gaps in US military intelligence sharing and delays in deliveries of American interceptor missiles. US officials have denied deliberately disrupting these services.What is Starshield and how does it affect Ukraine?Starshield is a military-grade satellite communications system developed by SpaceX, the company owned by Elon Musk. It is a more advanced sister system to Starlink, which is widely used by Ukrainian forces for communications and drone operations.European countries pay for Ukraine's access to Starshield. However, the advanced system is not available to all Ukrainian troops. Many units rely on it to operate drones while using standard Starlink connections for basic communications.Ukrainian officials have reported slowdowns affecting both Starshield and Starlink.Musk has said that Starshield is controlled by the Pentagon. However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio added to the confusion when he said on Wednesday that SpaceX determined access to both Starlink and Starshield.According to Ukrainian officials, the initial disruption caused drones to lose their connections at speeds as low as 40 miles per hour. Connectivity has since improved, but drones reportedly continue to lose their connections when travelling faster than 100 miles per hour.While some drone models can operate at these lower speeds, others need to fly faster to hit their targets, the report said.The restrictions have also affected interceptor drones used to bring down Russian drones targeting Ukrainian cities, Zelenskyy said.Ukraine is now looking for alternative ways to operate its drones, fearing that satellite connectivity could be restricted again or cut off entirely. Military commanders said the search for alternatives was diverting soldiers' attention from battlefield operations.US denies deliberately restricting satellite servicesUkrainian officials have sought clarification on who ordered the reported restrictions on Starshield and Starlink and why.A White House official told The New York Times that there had been no changes to satellite internet services in Ukraine.Trump also denied responsibility for any changes, saying on Friday that it “wasn’t me” and that “from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”Rubio said a day later that a Starlink slowdown in Ukraine had “sort of happened” but added that “my understanding is it’s been restored.”Zelenskyy has described the changes to Starshield as “a planned operation”.On NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said that “President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge.”The issue has also drawn criticism from US lawmakers across party lines, with calls for the Trump administration to restore Ukraine's satellite connectivity.After a group of lawmakers spoke with Zelenskyy over a video call on Monday, Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said the Ukrainian president had “confirmed ongoing Starlink disruptions, reported interruptions to critical US intelligence sharing and raised concerns about delays in air-defense interceptors.”Tillis also criticised Washington's approach towards Moscow, saying: “Degrading Ukraine’s satellite communications, weakening its air defenses and easing sanctions against Russia only embolden Putin and prolong this war.”He was referring to a move by Trump to allow the US to buy Russian diesel fuel.On Tuesday, Zelenskyy said he had a “substantive discussion” with Rubio about Starshield, shortages of missile interceptors and recent disruptions to early warning systems for Russian ballistic missile attacks.Rubio rejected claims that the US had withheld warnings about Russian attacks on Ukraine, calling them “simply not accurate”. He also said Patriot interceptors were in short supply worldwide.“Nothing is being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” Rubio said.Ukrainian troops struggle to adapt to restrictionsDespite the conflicting statements from Washington, Ukrainian commanders said the effects of the reported restrictions were evident on the battlefield.Brigadier General Andriy Biletsky, who recently took command of thousands of troops in the Center Grouping of Forces in eastern Ukraine, said Ukrainian forces were adapting to the new speed limits.Before the restrictions, Ukrainian drones using Starshield could fly at speeds of up to 250 miles per hour while maintaining a stable connection, Biletsky said.The formal speed limit had already been 100 miles per hour, but it had not been enforced, he added.This could allow the US to maintain that the system's rules had not changed, even as Ukrainian forces experienced a significant impact on the battlefield, the report said.Biletsky said that even if Ukraine managed to modify its attack drones to operate within the speed limits, interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered weapons would remain at a disadvantage.These interceptors need to fly faster than incoming drones to bring them down. Russian jet-powered drones can travel far faster than 100 miles per hour.“Reducing the speed limits for air defense is a painful decision that literally undermines the protection of our cities, first and foremost,” Biletsky said. “So when the Pentagon took this step, it was undoubtedly an unfriendly move toward Ukraine’s civilian population.”Ukrainian commanders told The New York Times that they believed the restrictions were the result of a political decision rather than a technical problem. They said troops had long feared that Washington could use satellite connectivity as leverage to push Kyiv into making concessions.Oleh recalled receiving a series of angry calls from soldiers as his drones fell from the sky last week. Troops scrambled to redirect the drones and save as much equipment as possible.He said soldiers felt abandoned and argued that Ukraine should stop viewing the US as an ally.Lieutenant Yuriy Butusov, a company commander with Ukraine's 23rd Assault Regiment in the Khartia Corps, said the slower connections had severely affected his troops' operations.He said the disruption had effectively given Russian forces “a vacation day”.“This day without Starlink saved many lives and many trucks for Russia, unfortunately,” Butusov said.“It’s a big cost for us,” he added. “And much more blood. Our blood.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: US embassy accuses Canada of brushing off allegations of election interference
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney dismissed the claim, noting that it was the that US initiated trade actions against Canada.
articles.body:
The US Embassy in Ottawa has accused Canadian officials of election meddling ahead of the November midterms.

The embassy said Canadian leaders have brushed off concerns over "potential interference", and that ministers and premiers "openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".

Canadian leaders, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, have dismissed the claims. Relations between the North American neighbours have hardened during second Trump administration.

The midterms will determine which political party controls both branches of the US Congress, which could have a significant impact on the rest of Donald Trump's presidency.

The fact sheet released by the US Embassy on Wednesday alleges the Canadian government "brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances".

It cites comments and actions, like meetings with US Democrats and calling for retaliatory tariffs against the US.

For example, it says that when Industry Minister Mélanie Joly was asked what she expected regarding tariffs if Democrats were to win midterm elections, she responded, "That's exactly why I'm meeting so many governors and potential presidential candidates."

Ontario Premier Doug Ford pushed Canada's federal government, it states, to consider additional retaliatory tariffs on imports from "politically significant states to the current administration's base of support".

Asked on Wednesday about the allegations, Carney noted that it was the US that first initiated trade actions against Canada.

"We've responded to those to protect Canadian jobs, to protect Canadian companies and develop our economy," Carney said.

He said his government's response has been "in the interests of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy".

Carney, who was announcing a nearly C$9bn ($6.2bn) aid package in response to US tariffs, was accompanied by both Joly and Ford.

Ford said that he has "no interest at all" in interfering in US elections.

"I'll tell you what the American people want. They want certainty, they want stability," Ford said, adding that he will focus on Ontario and Canada.

"The people of the United States will make that determination in the midterms," he said.

articles.title: U.S. is a big reason the world is losing ground in the fight against climate change, U.N. report says
articles.summary: The U.S. was the only major economy that failed last year to reduce its carbon pollution or at least slow the growth in how much carbon dioxide is spewed by burning fossil fuels.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says. If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will most likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday’s update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That’s about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year’s projections by the same science team. “This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas. “In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report. The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics, which measures countries’ climate-fighting plans. He was not part of the U.N. report but, like several other outside scientists, said it was scientifically sound. Shooting far past Paris climate goal The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate-fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year’s projection. Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact. The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees. The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.” Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen. “The report’s message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts, who was not part of the study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.” An added tenth of a degree of danger Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will most likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century. “This report shows that America’s retreat isn’t just a political embarrassment. It has real consequences for the planet and for millions of people around the world,” said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, a climate organization. “An extra tenth of a degree might sound insignificant, but in climate terms it is enormous. It means more dangerous heat waves, more destructive floods, more failed harvests and more lives lost. For vulnerable communities in Africa, already living on the front lines of the climate crisis, every fraction of a degree matters. These are not abstract numbers. They are human lives.” Hare said that extra one-tenth of a degree pushes an additional 140 million people “into dangerously hot conditions” and increases the odds of the collapse of the Amazon rainforest or ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica. It also would cost the world and shave about $1.2 trillion from the global economy, said University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann. And the U.S. effect is probably even bigger than what the United Nations calculates because if the world’s largest historical climate polluter doesn’t do much to fight global warming, other nations may ease off in their efforts as well, said Johan Rockstrom, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany. “The rest of the world is exhausted when it comes to counting the damage that the U.S. is willingly doing to allies, multilateral structures, economic cooperation, disaster relief,” Australian climate scientist Malte Meinshausen said. “The rest of the world should probably continue to focus even less on the U.S.”

articles.title: Anand Mahindra revisits Rishikesh memories, “I just hope that, amid all the changes, it holds on to its soul”; calls this restaurant his ‘practically my canteen’ during filmmaking days
articles.summary: Recently, ace industrialist Anand Mahindra shared his old memories that brought Rishikesh in Uttrakhand into the spotlight for a more personal reason.
articles.body: Recently, ace industrialist Anand Mahindra shared his old memories that brought Rishikesh in Uttrakhand into the spotlight for a more personal reason. In his #Sundaywanderer post on X on October 18, 2026, he revisited memories of his filmmaking days in the town. He recalled a restaurant where he regularly ate and the hills where he filmed a sadhu for his thesis film.It’s a fact that Rishikesh has long drawn travellers looking for different things from a holiday. For some, it is a place to sit beside the Ganga and meditate, for some it's a place they find peace and spirituality and listen to the river. For others, it is a destination for yoga, adventure and temple visits.For travellers, his personal memories of Rishikesh offered a reason to look beyond Rishikesh's familiar adventure activities.Sharing a few pictures, he wrote,“These pictures take me straight back to my filmmaking days. Chotiwala restaurant was practically my canteen while I was making my thesis film. And I’d head up into the hills behind Swargashram to film the sadhu, Bankhandi Baba.”Chotiwala restaurantBeing at Chotiwala restaurant and eating there is among the strongest memories Anand Mahindra shared. He described it as “practically my canteen” while making his thesis film. For travellers, the restaurant offers a chance to connect with a familiar part of Rishikesh's food and cultural landscape. Rather than treating the restaurant as just another stop on a sightseeing itinerary, visitors can make time to enjoy a meal and explore the surrounding streets.SwargashramSwargashram was another place Mahindra mentioned from his early filmmaking days. He recalled heading into the hills behind the area to film a sadhu named Bankhandi Baba. Located along the Ganga, it has ashrams, temples and yoga and spiritual studies centres. For those seeking a break from crowded tourist attractions, an unhurried walk through this area can be as rewarding as visiting the town's better-known landmarks.He further wrote, “Haven’t been back for a while. But Rishikesh seems to be getting quite a makeover! New riverfront walkways, spruced-up public spaces.”Triveni GhatA visit to Rishikesh is incomplete without witnessing the evening Ganga aarti at Triveni Ghat. The ceremony brings together priests, lamps, devotional chanting and visitors gathered along the riverbank. Triveni Ghat is one of the town's best-known bathing ghats, where pilgrims traditionally take a holy dip before visiting nearby temples. It is suggested to arrive early which allows one to find a place to sit and observe the surroundings.Beatles AshramBeatles Ashram is another prime highlight of Rishikesh's international appeal. In February 1968, members of the Beatles visited Maharishi Mahesh Yogi's ashram to learn transcendental meditation. The site, now popularly known as Beatles Ashram or Chaurasi Kutia.Visitors can explore its old meditation structures, forest surroundings and graffiti-covered walls. It offers a different perspective on the town, showing how Rishikesh became a meeting point for Indian spiritual traditions and international cultural influences.Riverfront walks on the Ganga“A welcome facelift for a town where nature has always done most of the decorating”, he writes further.The new riverfront walkways and improved public spaces mentioned by Anand Mahindra bring attention to another way of experiencing Rishikesh.For those seeking more action, Rishikesh is also known for white-water rafting, particularly around Shivpuri, approximately 19 km from the town. Rafting is one of the region's major adventure activities subject to local conditions and official permissions. Visitors should book through authorised operators and follow safety instructions.How to plan a trip to RishikeshThe period from mid-September to December is among the recommended times to visit. October can be particularly appealing for travellers who want to combine riverside walks, temple visits and outdoor activities. A two-day trip can cover Swargashram, Chotiwala restaurant, Triveni Ghat and Beatles Ashram, with additional time for rafting or other activities if conditions permit.Ending his posts, he throws light on the most important thing, the soul of Rishikesh:“But I just hope that, amid all the changes, Rishikesh holds on to its soul”.You use AI every day. articles.title: South Korea: Famed shark Bukangi returns to canal after failed rescue
articles.summary: Authorities had hoped the female shark would swim back to sea after being led out of the canal.
articles.body:
A famed dusky shark in South Korea has returned to the canal where she had been stuck for a month, just one day after authorities said they had successfully guided her out, local media report.

The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after she was spotted lingering in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.

South Korea's oceans ministry said on Wednesday evening they had led Bukangi out of the canal into an open harbour - but reports later said the shark had swum back to the mouth of the canal, having apparently broken through a barrier installed by authorities.

Another operation to relocate Bukangi has been scheduled for Thursday.

It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.

In recent weeks, more than 1.6 million visitors have descended upon a park in Busan to catch a glimpse of Bukangi, named after the canal in which she was spotted.

Her popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city has embraced her as an unofficial mascot.

But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as she appeared to be injured and was not eating. There were concerns that she would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.

In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.

Hundreds of adoring fans cheered and waved goodbye to their shark, unaware that she would still be lingering in the canal by the next day.

Before Wednesday's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.

articles.title: 50 years before E20, Tamil Nadu engineers did ethanol test drive
articles.summary: In the 1970s, researchers at the college of engineering, guindy, modified cars to run on 100% ethanol.
articles.body: In the 1970s, researchers at the college of engineering, guindy, modified cars to run on 100% ethanol. The technology showed promise, but concerns over fuel supply and food security stalled the project. Now, Anna University plans to get behind the wheelFive decades before ethanol blending became a national policy, engineers in Tamil Nadu had demonstrated that cars, two-wheelers and buses could run on the fuel.The experiment began in the 1970s, after petrol prices rose from ₹4 to ₹6 a litre in 1973. Faced with the prospect of rising fuel costs, the Tamil Nadu government asked professors at the Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) Laboratory of the College of Engineering, Guindy (CEG), to explore alternative fuels.A team led by Professor T R Jagadeesan modified petrol engines to run on 100% ethanol, replacing the carburettor, ignition system, and cooling and heating systems.“Ethanol is a good fuel for a petrol engine. It has a high flame speed and burns without producing black smoke,” says Jagadeesan. Its main drawback is mileage. “The heat energy produced using ethanol is only about 60% of that from petrol. And this affects mileage.”The difference was evident in the team’s road tests. In a 1979 trial, a car ran 7.2km per litre on ethanol, compared with 11.46km per litre on petrol. On highways, the corresponding figures were 9.38km per litre and 14.9km per litre. An Ambassador car given to the research team recorded 6.2km per litre on ethanol, against 9.54km per litre on petrol, in a city road test on January 21, 1980.The researchers found that engine modifications could improve ethanol’s performance. They increased the compression ratio of a Fiat car engine from 7:1 to 11:1 and modified its carburettor and other components. At the normal compression ratio, the ethanol-powered engine recorded a thermal efficiency of 26%, compared with 25% for petrol. With the higher compression ratio, efficiency rose to 32%.The team then tested the technology on a 2,000km run with two cars, travelling from Chennai to Ooty, on to Kanyakumari and back to Chennai. The vehicles negotiated hill roads and could be restarted at Ooty without difficulty.The project caught the attention of chief minister M G Ramachandran, who wanted Ambassador cars at the state secretariat to run on ethanol. Vehicles used by senior officials were soon operated on ethanol and brought to the Anna University laboratory for refuelling.The technology was also demonstrated to Prime Minister Indira Gandhi and finance minister R Venkataraman. The demonstrations generated interest, but the project did not receive approval for large-scale implementation.“Perhaps we were ahead of our time,” says Jagadeesan.The main obstacle was the source of the fuel. At the time, ethanol production was closely linked to sugarcane. Using food-linked resources to produce fuel raised concerns over food security. Policymakers feared that an ethanol programme could divert agricultural produce away from consumption.The team also tested ethanol in diesel engines used by farmers and in a bus engine provided by Ashok Leyland. They achieved an 80% ethanol blend in a diesel motor pump set, while a 40% blend was achieved in the bus. Because ethanol and diesel do not blend easily, the two fuels were supplied separately.The research, conducted between 1975 and 1985, was presented at international forums in the UK, the US, Canada and Brazil.“We proved five decades ago that 100% ethanol could be used in modified petrol engines. Even after five years of testing, the engines showed no damage. The wear and tear was similar to what happens when petrol is used,” says Jagadeesan.Anna University now plans to revive the work, studying ethanol performance at different compression ratios, with a focus on flexible-fuel vehicles.“The case for ethanol as an alternative transport fuel has strengthened. Ethanol can now be produced from several sources, including agricultural residues, potentially reducing the pressure on food crops,” says V Kumaresan, registrar-in-charge.The university will also be part of an ethanol research project involving IIT Madras and universities in China and Brazil. The Tamil Nadu government has allotted a research grant of ₹5 lakh to the team.India’s ethanol routeIndia’s ethanol-blended petrol programme aims to improve energy security, support farmers and reduce environmental impacts while promoting the use of domestically produced renewable fuel.India’s E20 policy, introduced under the programme, is a nationwide mandate requiring fuel retailers to sell petrol blended with 20% ethanol and 80% gasoline. India has fast-tracked the nationwide rollout of E20 fuel, with ethanol blending increasing from less than 1.5% in 2013–14 to 20% in 2025–26, five years ahead of schedule. The move, though, has raised concerns that it will lower fuel efficiency, accelerate corrosion and damage components not designed for higher ethanol content.India imports more than 80% of the crude oil it consumes. Ethanol produced from Indian sugarcane, maize and rice offers a way to reduce that exposure by using resources grown at home.Ethanol blending is a globally accepted practice. Several major economies, such as the US, Brazil and Japan, have incorporated ethanol into their fuel strategies.Ethanol blending: Pros and consPROS: Cuts crude oil imports and saves foreign exchange; gives farmers and distilleries a steady, assured buyer for surplus grain, sugarcane and maize; burns cleaner than petrol.CONS: Lower energy content can mean lower mileage; food-versus-fuel concerns remain—the same worry that held back the Tamil Nadu experiment. articles.title: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
articles.summary: Governments and companies are scrambling to protect their websites, as Amazon says it experienced attacks before the warning was made public.
articles.body:
The UK government says it is working to actively identify and patch any potential exposure in its online services, after vulnerabilities were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites.

Governments and some of the world's biggest companies, including Amazon, were scrambling to protect their systems on Thursday before hackers could exploit them.

The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments and agencies urged websites to address them.

Amazon was targeted in multiple attempts, which it said occurred before an embargo on the warning was lifted. It added that it was unclear how actors knew about the vulnerabilities.

A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.

"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note .

Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October.

In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said.

The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said.

While the PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch", details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.

In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said.

The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning.

The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added.

The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days".

She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said.

The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade.

Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure.

What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber security scramble?

The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website.

This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed. PHP released software patches that could be used to address the flaws on 21 October.

The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified, "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database".

It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update.

OpenAI called the discovery, "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

Websites taken down worldwide as critical cyber-security update issued
